claims.text: A supervised machine-learning framework combined with systematic design of experiments can isolate and quantify the effects of individual Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr fractions on mechanical properties.
The proposed framework will enable prediction and optimization of mechanical performance.
The initial alloy is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The initial alloy is fully consolidated and homogenized after powder-metallurgy or arc-melting processing.
Systematically varying elemental atomic fractions and testing the resulting alloys can distinguish individual constituent effects.
Controlling sample preparation and oxygen content reduces confounding effects in mechanical-property comparisons.
Variations in elemental composition alter alloy microstructure.
Elemental variations alter phase distributions, lattice distortion, and grain size in HfNbTaTiZr-based alloys.
Composition-induced microstructural changes affect yield strength and ductility.
ML regression or neural networks can reveal the effect of each atomic-percent shift on solid-solution strengthening, lattice distortion, and phase stability.
Solid-solution strengthening, lattice distortion, and phase stability mediate correlations between composition and mechanical performance.
Individual element contents will exhibit distinct trends with strength and ductility.
Increasing certain constituent elements may promote solid-solution strengthening and produce moderate to strong improvements in hardness and yield strength.
The near-equiatomic alloy provides the reference for evaluating composition-dependent mechanical-property changes.
Extreme departures from near-equiatomic composition may introduce additional phases.
Additional phases caused by extreme composition changes may reduce straightforward ML predictive accuracy.
The individual mechanical-property roles of Hf, Nb, and Ta are not fully resolved.
A factorial composition series spanning 5–35 at.% in 5 at.% steps can be used to test the ML predictions.
Hardness, tensile properties, XRD, and SEM/EDS measurements can evaluate the predicted mechanical and microstructural responses.
Failure of measured properties to correlate with ML predictions across the composition range would not support robust quantification of elemental effects by the model.
